subtopic: SEALS-DEPLETION OF HERD-OPERATIONS OF NORWEGIAN VESSELS
SEALS-DEPLETION OF HERD-OPERATIONS OF NORWEGIAN VESSELS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a short statement on recent developments in the seal hunt. It will answer several questions asked in recent days by hon. members and serve to bring the house up to date on the situation both in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and on the Labrador front in the North Atlantic.
There is real concern from a conservation point of view. The seal count, to date, has been small both in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and off Labrador. In the Gulf the count of adult female seals has been in the order of
only 250,000. In a normal year this figure would have been between 750,000 and one million. It follows that less than one-third as many adult female seals have been observed in the Gulf of St. Lawrence as compared to normal times.
The quota set by regulation for the taking of young seals, as hon. members know, is 50,000. It is 50,000 assuming a normal year in so far as adult females are concerned. This year we terminated the hunt at 35,000, our main concern being that, if the hunt had been allowed to continue for another day, an entire year class may have been wiped out.
The main problem on the Gulf of St. Lawrence has been the absence of ice suitable to the pupping of young seals. This, together with frequent storms has resulted in many drownings. The young seals have been drowned either at birth or as a result of the breaking up of the small ice floes which have been limited mainly to the Northumberland Strait between Prince Edward Island and the mainland.
The hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) has quoted local fishermen as saying that there are a large number of seals off the north coast of Prince Edward Island. I regret to advise the house that there are no more than 6,000 young seals in the entire area at the present time.
The second phase of the hunt, Mr. Speaker, is now concentrated on the front off Labrador in the North Atlantic. The main seal concentration is around the mouth of Hamilton Inlet. Six Canadian ships are taking young seals there at the present time. Fourteen Norwegian vessels are also in this same general area.
I regret to inform the house that we have encountered some difficulties with the Norwegian sealers. When the season opened on the front on March 12 several Norwegian ships were observed inside our territorial waters. One is definitely known to have been taking seals on Saturday, March 15. Warnings were immediately issued by radio to all Norwegian vessels ordering them not to take seals and instructing them to leave Canadian waters.
[DOT] (11:10 a.m.)
Due to extreme weather conditions, thick ice and heavy Arctic fog, it was impossible

March 21. 1969
Depletion of Seal Herds for our fisheries protection vessel, the Cape Freels, to get into this area. We therefore requested the Department of Transport icebreaker, Sir Humphrey Gilbert to come up from St. John's, Newfoundland. This vessel, with a helicopter and fisheries protection officers aboard is now in Hamilton Inlet with instructions to pick up the Norwegian vessel, which was known to be taking seals on Saturday, if it is still within our 12 mile limit. Otherwise it would appear that the situation on the front is generally under control, as all the other Norwegian vessels are known to be outside of our territorial waters.
I should reiterate, in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that our fisheries protection service is operating under very adverse conditions off Labrador. Lack of visibility, freezing of ships in the ice, high winds and poor radio communications have contributed to delays which have been encountered in carrying out orders which were issued some days ago.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: SEALS-DEPLETION OF HERD-OPERATIONS OF NORWEGIAN VESSELS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister's statement just recently came to my attention. I have not had a chance to study it. The members of this house were interested to hear what the minister had to say regarding the seal herd in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. I believe hon. members realize the importance of the seal hunt as a supplementary source of income to the fishermen in the Atlantic provinces.
The minister referred to the fact that the herd this year is very seriously depleted. I believe he mentioned the herd was down to
250,000	from 700,000. This is a real cause for concern, Mr. Speaker; but the minister omitted to mention the fact that Canada is now a member of ICNAF, the International Convention of the North Atlantic Fisheries. I believe this matter has been under the jurisdiction of ICNAF since 1966. Steps should be taken in ICNAF to ensure proper methods of conservation of the herd off the front. I believe that proper conservation methods must be taken with the main herd off the coast of Labrador. We can talk all we want about a sanctuary in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, but it is all to no avail unless the main herd is protected.
I am sure hon. members are glad to hear that the minister at last has his facts correct regarding the infringement of our Territorial waters that took place last weekend, and is still taking place, by Norwegian vessels. I brought this to the attention of the minister and his parliamentary secretary gave a reply on Monday. The reply by the minister on Tuesday indicated there was no evidence that

seals were being taken by the Norwegians. This was totally at variance with the reply given by his parliamentary secretary the previous Monday. We now find there is evidence the Norwegians were hunting seals within the three mile limit, and the department has had to request a coast-guard vessel to be dispatched from St. John's, several hundred miles distant. This highlights the inadequacy of the fleet of fisheries patrol vessels to enforce Canadian jurisdiction and conservation in our territorial waters, particularly in so far as fisheries and the seal herd are concerned.
The fleet of the Department of Fisheries patrol vessels must be substantially increased so the department can enforce our territorial jurisdiction. The seal fishery has been a subject of debate in this house for a number of years, more particularly since films produced in 1964 were shown around the world, and as a consequence of which Canada's reputation has suffered.
Canadians have been portrayed abroad as being a bunch of sadistic, barbarous people skinning baby seals alive, whereas in actual fact seals are humanely killed. The minister has in fact announced from first hand evidence that seals are humanely killed. I think he would be the first to admit that the killing of these animals is a necessary supplementary source of income for the fishermen of the Atlantic region. A request has been made in the house, and in writing to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, to have the whole matter aired before the committee, in order that the facts may be ascertained once and for all.

subtopic: SEALS-DEPLETION OF HERD-OPERATIONS OF NORWEGIAN VESSELS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to hear the announcement of the minister and to learn that the very unfortunate circumstances with regard to the seal herd in the Gulf of St. Lawrence had decreased as rapidly as they have. I had the opportunity of visiting that area with the minister. The area of ice off Prince Edward Island was very small in size and I think an accurate count was fairly easy to take. If there are only 6,000 pups left in the area, I think the minister is to be congratulated for terminating the seal hunt. The prime interest in this matter, leaving aside the ballyhoo and all the other propaganda in which certain people have been interested, should be the conservation of the sealing industry. The fact that an accurate count could be made indicates that something happened in the last
March 21, 1969

year, not only because of weather and fisheries conditions but with the seals themselves, because only a quarter of a million seals came into the gulf when normally there have been a million in the area.
We must make some arrangements through ICNAF or perhaps under a bilateral agreement with Norway as to the taking of seals on the front, because this year seals, rather than coming into the gulf, stayed on the front. The loss of three-quarters of a million seals is a very serious blow to the industry and will be a serious loss if it continues in the future.
I am surprised at the comments of some hon. members who have argued the matter on economic grounds. We are concerned here with an industry and the fact that conservation is more important than this year's catch. If those involved in the industry are in difficulty, and difficulty to our economy has developed1, the situation should be handled as an emergency and the government should provide financial assistance to the people involved. But we should not forfeit our right to carry on a reasonable conservation program. Ouir prime interest should be to maintain- the seal herd at a level which will allow harvesting for years to come. The minister will have serious difficulty, and this has been pointed out by other members of the house, with regard to the 12-mile limit and the headland to headland system. There will be difficulty in drawing our boundaries in this respect. Our discussions with Norway in this regard should not only be with the fishermen in the area but at government level in order that we can arrive at a bilateral agreement and conserve seals on the front as well as in the gulf.

subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND FORESTRY, AND OTHER NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have
enjoyed the interesting debate on the setting up of the new Department of Regional Economic Expansion. Before commenting on the department I should like to spend a few minutes outlining some great economic problems facing Canada today.
We in this great country are fortunate to be living at peace with our neighbours and the world. Canada is a very rich nation and our standard of living is one of the highest in the world. Despite our great wealth, abundant resources and high standard of living, there are still many serious social problems which we have not solved. We have in our country widespread poverty, great regional disparities and a disgraceful unemployment rate. A brief outline of these problems might serve as a background for the need to set up the new department.
These problems will not all be solved by the measures contemplated in this bill to reorganize the departments of government. There is widespread poverty in Canada. The fifth annual review of the Economic Council of Canada outlines it very clearly. In fact, it clearly sets out the picture in a 37-page review of the problem. The leading paragraph on this subject reads as follows:
Poverty in Canada is real. Its numbers are not in the thousands, but the millions. There is more of it than our society can tolerate, more than our economy can afford, and far more than existing measures and efforts can cope with. Its persistence, at a time when the bulk of Canadians enjoy one of the highest standards of living in the world, is a disgrace.
I would like to give a few facts on the extent of poverty in our nation. The lowest 20 per cent of non-farm families received an average annual income in 1965 of $2,263, representing 6.7 per cent of the total income for that year. The average should have been 20 per cent. The next 20 per cent received an average income of $4,542, or 13.4 per cent of the total income.
An answer to a question in the house not too long ago indicated there had been a very recent survey by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics which indicated that 2,753,000 wage earners earn less than $3,000 per year. In reply to the same question the information was given that 997,000 wage earners in Canada have annual incomes between $3,000
March 21, 1969

Government Organization and $4,000. These figures indicate that 3,750,000 wage earners, 55 per cent of the total, earn less than $4,000 per year. I agree that income statistics do not give us the entire picture, but they are a very good criterion as to how widespread the problem of poverty is.
There are interesting facts on the problem of regional disparity, the solving of which is one of the main objectives in the new legislation. The latest records for which we have adequate statistics set out quite clearly the terrible difference which exists between various regions in- Canada. This is a good time to put the figures on the record again.
In the most recent period for which statistics are available, 1962-64, personal income per capita was $2,025 in Ontario, $1,521 in Quebec, $1,302 in Nova Scotia, $1,167 in New Brunswick, $1,115 in Prince Edward Island, and $1,007 in Newfoundland. This clearly indicates the need for action on the problem of regional disparity. The people of the province with the lowest income receive less than half the per capita income of the people of the province with the best income.
The next point I would like to raise in connection with the subject of poverty is unemployment. As other speakers have pointed out, we have been made aware of this by the Economic Council of Canada. On numerous occasions the council has urged the government to set a maximum limit of not more than 3 per cent. Currently more than 6 per cent of our working force is unemployed. In areas such as the Atlantic provinces the figure is over 10 per cent. In the province of Quebec it is over 8 per cent. In my own province of British Columbia it is well over 6 per cent. This, again, is a tragedy so far as Canada is concerned.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
We have three problems in this respect, over-all poverty, the extreme disparity between regions, and unemployment, upon which we are all trying to focus attention. Having briefly outlined these problems I should like to discuss one or two aspects of setting up the new Department of Regional Economic Expansion. Again, Mr. Chairman, I point out to hon. members and the minister in particular that just changing the name of the department will not bring success. We must be prepared to make major changes in our approach to these problems. We must make major changes in a variety of fields.

This department could play a major role in solving many of the economic problems facing us at the present time, especially those involving regional disparity in- areas where sufficient economic expansion has not taken place. I say again that unless the government is prepared to make drastic changes in- its former plans and policies the new department will fall far short of the goals which everyone would like to see achieved.
In 1963 the government carried out a reorganization of departments. The results were not very beneficial, and now another reshuffle is to take place. For example, Bill C-173 brings industry, trade and commerce together in one department. They should never have been separated in the first instance. However, I hope that the reorganization of a number of government departments will result in more co-ordination and efficiency than we have experienced in the past.
The idea of one department being responsible for attempting to eliminate regional economic disparities is a sound one. Our party has been urging it for years. It could at least prevent the costly duplication of attempted services by a number of different agencies. The minister himself showed how costly the lack of co-ordinated action has been so far as the Canadian taxpayers are concerned. The minister pointed out that since 1963 we have spent over $1 billion on various programs, and he estimated we have wasted about half this amount.
As I said before, for years our party has called for over-all direction, -co-ordination and planning in every government program so as to make them fully effective. There has never been such co-ordination, as the minister frankly admits. The federal government has never allocated sufficient financial resources to really come -to grips with the problem of regional disparity. Now that one department will be in charge of and responsible for such programs, I have no hesitation in endorsing -the legislation setting up the department.
The increase in departmental expenditures of approximately $37 million this year means -there will not be too great a departure from past policies and programs which have attempted to deal with regional disparities. This must be -apparent to everyone, because if more regions are to be brought under the plan the budget should be sharply increased in order to meet the correspondingly greater need.
March 21, 1969	COMMONS
I would like now to speak very generally about the new Department of Regional Economic Expansion. The department is to take over the designated area program and several other federal programs such as ARDA, the Atlantic Development Board, etc. We find that the total budget for 1969-70 is almost $192 million which represents an increase of $37 million over last year when we add the amounts which were allocated to the various programs being brought under the plan.
We find that under the designated area program established under the old legislation benefits were available for secondary processing or manufacturing industries but not for primary industries. Benefits under the designated area program, which I understand will be in effect for some time even under the new legislation, included capital costs amounting to one-third of those under $250,000, one-quarter of those under $1 million, and one-fifth of those over $1 million to a maximum of $5 million. They also included depreciation allowance.
Under the designated area program there was no assistance for the tourist industry. I understand this is being considered under the new legislation. I am convinced that the tourist industry should be included in any new plan because it has tremendous potential in many areas which are currently classed as regions of disparity. I urge that it be included in the regulations which will be set up under the new department.
For the new department to be successful it must avoid the obvious mistakes made in the past because of the lack of a planned and co-ordinated policy. For the new department to be successful there must be full co-ordination at three levels of government. There must be full co-ordination at the federal level. In my opinion, this entails three distinct steps. First, I believe there should be a formulation and consideration of consistent programs as they affect or are directed toward regionally balanced growth. Second, there must be communication and delegation of authority to federal regional departments. This is essential in a country as vast as ours and it will cut the red tape often found in a central office. If we do not have communication and delegation of authority to federal regional departments, we will find that the program will not be as effective as it should be.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
The third point is that there must be a meshing together of specific operations by federal departments and agencies within a

Government Organization region. Again I repeat that this is absolutely essential for full results. Let me give one example. It does not apply to the new department which has not yet been set up. I have been dealing with a problem in the Creston area where three federal government departments were doing various jobs. On checking with the departments I found that each of them does not know what the others have been doing or what their object is in spending money in a certain area. To me this is nonsense and is one of the reasons that many of our programs have failed miserably in the past.
The second area of co-operation must be at the provincial level, and again I contend that this is another necessary ingredient for the success of the program. I feel it is absolutely essential. If there is a failure to co-ordinate the provincial and federal roles in the setting up of projects and the carrying out of programs, we will find that the result will be little short of disastrous. I suggest also that provincial agencies, especially in the regional areas affected, must also be delegated sufficient authority to deal quickly and adequately with most problems. In my view this is a lesser problem at the provincial than at the federal level.
The third area where there must be full co-operation is at the regional and municipal level. Again, to be successful the programs must have the co-operation and the backing of the various municipal and regional groups in the entire area. This includes, of course, the various organizations in these designated areas. In addition to having the support of the organizations they must have the backing of the general public.
I should like to make it clear that I feel the inescapable alternative to effective consultation and co-ordination among the federal, provincial and municipal levels is conflict, confusion, waste, frustration and the ultimate failure of the policy. There must be continous and effective liaison between the federal and provincial levels if the program outlined by the minister is to be fully successful. There are a number of other problems which I would like to raise in connection with regional development. I do not think you can just outline a series of programs unless you are prepared to take other steps. Canada needs a great deal of capital to help finance some of these projects. This is where the need for a Canada Development Corporation arises. The corporation could make sure that funds were

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am very pleased to be able to say a few words in this debate.
I was very glad that the previous speaker was given a few extra minutes because it indicates that the house is in a rather genial mood today, as it was all day yesterday when the majority of speakers from all parties were allowed a few minutes beyond their allotted time. I think this is a good thing because the legislation before us is most important.
Before proceeding with my remarks I would like to say to the minister that some weeks ago when we were discussing other legislation in the house which the minister was piloting the minister, as the result of some unkind words I said regarding his activities in connection with that legislation, became rather disturbed and irked and his blood pressure went up, as does the blood pressure of most of us at such times. However, today he looks calm and collected and does not appear to be upset. In fact he is genial and serene, and I hope he will not take anything I say too much to heart.
I do not intend to go into great detail on this legislation dealing with the new Department of Regional Economic Expansion other than to point out that if the elimination of economic disparities is desirable it is equally desirable that all the tools for that purpose be placed in the same hands. So far as the minister is concerned, this bill places the tools in his hands. It remains to be seen whether he can finish the job. Even if he only starts it, that will be something.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
The bill is a perfect example of the way in which government action leads to an increasing commitment of public funds with no appreciable increase in benefits. However, no one objects to a commitment of public funds as long as we get results. The department, as would appear from the estimates for 1969-70, seems to include what formerly came under ARDA and P.F.R.A., plus a few other scattered programs, with the National Capital Commission thrown in as political makeweight, the Cape Breton Development Corporation, some remnants of the Department of Labour not quite defunct, and various powers and authorities formerly under the Department of Industry. It will also include the Atlantic Development Board which now finds itself reduced to being a mere sounding
March 21, 1969

board. In pursuance of this reorganization the new department will, we are told:
1.	Encourage economic expansion in regions where growth is lagging.
2.	Prepare development plans and programs.
3.	Recommend special areas for action to improve economic growth.
4.	Enter into agreements with the provinces to provide for economic expansion.
5.	Build up the economic infrastructure of areas.
6.	Provide special incentives to commercial undertakings.
These various programs will cost Canadian taxpayers approximately $150 million this year-evidence of a fairly dramatic expansion. Under this government we have seen the inauguration of direct grants to industries through the area development incentives program, and in 1967 the ceiling was raised to $200 million.
The hon. member for Halton yesterday spoke about the migration of young people from the Atlantic provinces. I shall have something to say about that, but before doing so may I comment that the present government spawns new departments like mushrooms in a damp basement. Problems cannot be solved simply by changing nameplates on doors. Nothing has been done for our young people. There has been no leadership, no policy. We see a generation of young people whom we have allowed to be assaulted by narcotics, bombarded by propaganda, overcome by violence, intimidated by mobs. And we think we have done right by them. Meanwhile, the government goes on walking in its sleep.
In spite of constant reorganization and reshuffling, no attention has been paid to the challenge of youth, none to the demands for the expansion and development of natural resources. The most serious situation in this country today is that created by the lack of challenge for young people. This bill does not deal with the problem. It adds nothing new. It takes existing divisions and sections and rearranges them. This is the third or fourth government reorganization since 1963. We have seen reorganization piled upon reorganization, reshuffling on top of reshuffling. The Department of Industry came on the scene with a great fanfare of trumpets. It has apparently been a colossal failure and is to be buried within the Department of Trade and
Government Organization Commerce. Now we are setting up a department which is to carry on the policy of making grants to industries to enable them to establish themselves in certain areas or to stay in areas where they are already established. The news handout from the minister's office puts it this way:
The area development incentives program is to continue, but additional assistance will be available if special circumstances make it necessary to help a commercial undertaking establish, expand, or modernize in a special area. Such additional assistance will be available only if it is essential to the implementation of a development plan.
This seems to imply that there are some reservations. The suggestion is that the area development program will go on and that grants will be made to industry though perhaps under more restrictions than formerly. In the case of a department which will be spending large amounts of public money it is well not to begin operations under reservations or without a clear idea of what is entailed, what the purposes are, and what methods are to be followed. After all, the policy behind this department is one of direct intervention in and interference with the economy. There is nothing new in this. It is being done in the form of incentives rather than by way of compulsion. If it were being done by compulsion, it would amount to straight regimentation. Instead, it may represent a kind of fiscal regimentation. Whatever the philosophy behind it is, we should be clear about the likely effects of what is proposed. This is one of the problems raised by the bill before us; there is no clear indication of how effective the procedure is likely to prove.
Let us face the fact that under the area development incentives programs brought in by the government 18 months ago the procedure proved ineffective. We know it has been ineffective because the minister said so himself. Yet this same procedure is now to be employed by the new department. The area development incentives program is to be carried on, according to the statement from the minister's office, and direct grants are to be made to industrial organizations to persuade them to do what the government thinks they should be doing. This is a situation calculated to cause some misgiving in the light of the minister's statement during the federal-provincial constitutional conference. I draw attention to the following report which appeared in the Globe and Mail of February 13, not long ago:
The Area Development Act provides for grants to industries which establish in sections designated by the federal government as slow growth areas.
March 21, 1969

Government Organization
Mr. Marchand said the legislation had not worked as expected. Some industries which had benefited from the incentives would have moved to the area without them. Others had overexpanded as a result of the incentives.
The minister will no doubt remember -those remarks and certainly those who witnessed' his appearance on television will recall them. I continue to quote from this account in order to refresh his memory:
Mr. Marchand said the federal government's future regional development programs would concentrate on identifying regional growth centres and stress development in them.
He said the policy would mean that other small centres in the same region could not expect the same assistance and called on the provincial premiers to help him sell the program to the people.
Further, the article states-this is very interesting and I am reading it because of its importance:
We need political strength to resist pressure. All the villages, all the small towns in Canada want to have industries, want us to spend money for infrastructure, and so forth-
Previous federal efforts in regional development had often spread money too thinly and tried to cover too large a territory. It was necessary to take into account natural economic forces and concentrate efforts in a few natural growth centres.
This gives an idea of the approach being taken by the minister and his department. It is an interesting and significant one and it is of great relevance to the -consideration of this -bill. For two years, according to -the minister, we have been- following an- accelerated program of handing out money to industry for the purpose of stimulating expansion in slow growth areas. The program has not worked because industries are in many cases more interested in suiting their own requirements than in participating in government economic plans. This is not entirely unexpected. In effect, the minister is saying that despite the fact his policy -and programs did not achieve the desired result they are to be repeated on an even bigger scale. At least, this is what it sounds like. I hope this is not really what the minister is saying because I have too much respect for the hon. gentleman as a man of constructive ideas, and as a trade unionist, to want to see him led down the garden path.
Surely we should be able to get a clearer picture from the minister and the department. We have been told, in effect, that to a large extent industry will go its own way regardless of government incentives which may be offered. Today, it appears that the government, or its experts, or the brains behind the minister, have decided that because of the

difficulties attached to getting industry to conform to patterns laid down in Ottawa, the department is to select certain areas where growth is already manifesting itself and move in there. This looks to me like following the path of least resistance. Surely it ought not -to take a whole new department and the expenditure of hundreds of millions of dollars to decide we should go into natural growth areas, areas in which I presume growth is already taking place, to spend money.
The minister asked the premiers to help him sell the program to the people. I am asking the minister to sell the program to this house, to dispel some of the doubts engendered by his own statements and by statements emanating from his department.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
I would also like -to hear what -the minister means by economic infrastructure. That phrase appears in his statement and in the statement issued by his department and, like charity, it seems to cover a multitude of sins. It is important that we should all be talking about the same things. I would like to know, in addition to the grants to industry, grants to provinces and arrangements with provinces, what additional undertakings are implied by the word "infrastructure". How far is the government going under this legislation? What kind of economic infrastructure is envisaged? Are we talking about facilities, transport, roads, railways? I think we should be very clear on what we -are discussing, and I would ask the minister to deal with some of these points when he -replies.
What we should have is a very clear picture of how these powers will be applied and how these functions will be exercised. We were able to spend very large -sums in the last few years without securing the desired results, but let us not repeat that process. If we are going to simply fallow -the line of least resistance and go where growth already exists and industries are already established, then where is the case for this new department?
One of the dangerous and negative developments in this government has been to allow nature to take its course and simply speed up the process. That is not policy; it is simply greasing the skids, as the government is doing in the case of the eastern Canada farmer.
This is another area where the government has fallen down completely. Again we have organization and reorganization. We have had
March 21. 1969	COMMONS
enough paper programs to ensure the prosperity of the paper industry for many years . to come, but little assistance for the farmer. The way in which farmers in Ontario, Quebec and the Atlantic provinces have been written off under this government's policies is an utter scandal. In pursuit of the policy of creating an urban proletariat the government has given the eastern farmer the choice between starving or lining up in city welfare offices. We now have the most recent study of the Atlantic Development Board forecasting further declines in agriculture in the Atlantic provinces. We did not need a special study to tell us what everybody knew. This government is now specializing in the obvious. It is all right to produce study upon study, report upon report, task force after task force, reorganization after reorganization, but when are we going to have some solutions? Farming in the Atlantic provinces has been reduced by half the number of farms since 1961. Is this a record of which the government can be proud? Their whole policy is negative and destructive. It does not require genius and the expenditure of millions to tell the farmers to get off the farm. The government should be producing policies to help the farmer stay on the farm, such as the establishment of agricultural institutions and vocational training schools in rural areas, building better roads, giving assistance in marketing products and so on.
No one can tell me that a farm family is better off on welfare, adding to the total of urban poor, than on their own land. Yet the policies of this government have followed the incredibly fatuous course of thinking that the farm problem can be solved by adding to the urban poor. They have now decided that the problem of the urban poor can be solved by wiping out government housing projects. They have decided the problem of slow growth can be solved by concentrating on the fast growth areas.
This government produces high-sounding policies and programs, the net result of which is to aid and abet the destruction of our society. The government has done absolutely nothing about the rural poor, the urban poor, the homeless, the farmer on his land a prey to the high-tax, high-spending inflation spawned by a government incredibly mediocre in performance and execution. Canada cannot long stand being saddled with policies having as their aim the destruction of a whole class of people, the self-employed in this nation.

When one considers that, according to the Atlantic Development Board, the total number of maritime farms decreased from 52,600 to 24,700 in the ten years prior to 1966, then one has an idea of the scope of the problem. We have had huge, pretentious, expensive programs aimed at the eastern Canada farmer, programs that remained largely paper programs, and the best thing the government hs has been able to do is to tell the farmer to get off the farm and line up in a welfare office in the city. The same course is being followed in the Atlantic provinces with regard to the fishing industry.
It does not take massive programs and huge commitments of funds simply to follow the current; we have got to have development programs. What we need is a department and a minister to push such programs, particularly in the Atlantic provinces and Quebec.
Achievement will not result from simply following the line of least resistance. I say to the minister that success in this field will not come instantly. It will be a long and perhaps painful process. It can be achieved only by orienting in one administrative capacity the various authorities required to bring about profound economic transformation. The minister is being given the power; I know he will do everything he can to use it constructively and wisely.
By this bill, as I understand it, the minister is given authority over agricultural development through ARDA, P.F.R.A., Maritime marshland rehabilitation, the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act, and so on. He will thus be responsible for rural development and will have the legislative power and authority to produce effective programs. He will have the power to encourage industry to go into areas where it is needed to provide employment. He will have the facilities to bring about widespread economic rehabilitation of lagging areas.
In the exercise of those powers, in the eradication of rural blight and the stimulation of economic expansion, the minister can count on the sympathy and understanding of every member of this house, particularly those from the Atlantic provinces where unfortunately regional disparity has its home. In that respect I must express my regret at the downgrading of the Atlantic Development Board and its demotion to an advisory body. I hope the minister will see fit to give every encouragement to this body to examine into and recommend solutions to the economic problems of the maritime and Atlantic region.
March 21, 1969

Government Organization I should like to say to the minister, through you, Mr. Chairman, that I was most pleased to hear of his appointment of Professor Smith as chairman of the new board.
We have seen what can be done in the example of the way Sysco has been functioning under provincial management. To the uninitiated, Sysco is the Sydney Steel Corporation, a crown corporation set up by the Nova Scotia provincial government. Perhaps with the full power of this legislation behind him the minister can take steps to bring that about.
At this time I should like publicly to go on record as lauding the accomplishments and being very enthused about the efforts of the steelworkers at the steel plant in Sydney, as well as the union and management. In conclusion I should like to say to the minister that once the department is launched and commences operation I hope he and the department will not embark upon a great series of studies, because it is doubtful whether any area of the earth's surface has been studied as much as have the maritime provinces by successive federal governments. There have been studies on every aspect of flora and fauna of the Atlantic and maritime provinces. There have been oyster studies, shrimp studies, frozen groundfish studies, bloater studies, studies on coal, on the tourist industry, on family formation, on agriculture, on every aspect of social and economic life in those historic provinces. We have been practically studied to death. As a newsman stated the other day when writing about these studies, the poor lobster has been studied so many times by successive governments that this has caused the lobster when mobile to move in reverse.

It would not be accurate to say that the studies have produced nothing. They have produced mountains of paper. The maritimes would have benefited more from government action if the government had decided to bring about even a 20 per cent reduction in freight rates. We did not need all these studies. According to a return tabled the other day in answer to a question by the tireless hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North on the subject of studies, hundreds of economic and social studies have been undertaken since confederation. In the field of agriculture there have been 54, in fisheries, 38, in rural development and forestry, 22, and in trade and commerce, 4. Two transportation studies have been undertaken and we have had 13 royal commissions and other commissions. Altogether there have been 133 studies, reports, commissions and investigations of one kind or another in the Atlantic region since confederation.
Before I resume my seat may I say to the minister: for heaven's sake, do not begin another series of studies and task forces. Surely the government has enough information to be able to act. We want the minister and his new department to bring about a rejuvenation of the Atlantic provinces, and our people will assist him in his task. We want industry and we want assistance, but do not think of us as poor cousins who want to cry on the shoulders of the rest of Canada. The Atlantic provinces have contributed to confederation in a great many ways. I wish the Minister every success in his endeavours with his new department and look forward to his co-operation.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to say a few words about this bill and to commend the government for having introduced it. I think I should first state that I am quite happy to see the very wide powers which are being given to the minister. I am glad this legislation does not tie him down too much as
DEBATES	6961
Government Organization previous legislation tied down ministers responsible for regional development.
Before getting into the burden of my remarks I would like to say a few words about the former area development agency and to indicate some of the difficulties associated with it, particularly as they affected my constituency and the region from which I come. My first criticism is that it was far too inflexible a piece of legislation. Boundaries were set by the Canada Manpower agency boundaries, and often these had little or nothing to do with the economic regions around them. Consequently a variety of situations arose in which bordering areas lost employment and manpower to areas which, through a quirk of fate, came under the area development agency.
In addition, the former A.D.A. did not take into consideration the local resources which were available in the various regions. It was a universal program. It was not really designed to seek out areas which had something to offer if only they could get a spark of help. It was reasonably successful in rural areas which happened to be designated in isolation and had no competing areas near them.
My third criticism of this program is that it was directed almost wholly to urban and industrial areas and did not really take into consideration the difficulties which rural communities have in attempting to attract some form of development to them. It is a fact that the program was most successful in those areas which were close to urban communities that had a substantial urban industrial base.
I know that when the minister took office in his new portfolio the first thing he did was to amend the A.D.A. legislation in such a way as to permit growth centres within regions to participate in the area development program. I think it is a legitimate criticism of the former program that where you had a growth centre in a particular region it was excluded from the benefits available under the area development agency. This situation has now been corrected. Now that growth centres seem to be the latest economic panacea we will see if this idea works as well as its professorial theorists seem to think it will.
I understand that new legislation will be brought down, hopefully by the end of June, to redesign the area development agency program. I hope that when this legislation does appear it will be far more flexible than the former legislation. The reason for this is simply that all parts of Canada are not equal. In
March 21, 1969

Government Organization the regional distinctions which must be made, or in the provincial distinctions, there are a variety of conditions with which the legislation must deal. I think one example will suffice to show this. That example would be the situation in the maritime provinces, say, Nova Scotia, where almost all of Nova Scotia with the exception of Halifax was designated under the former legislation. Now that Halifax has been included, I think the program has a chance of being some good to Nova Scotia.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
But in the area of northwestern Ontario, which is part of a very large province, there was no designation at all, and because great areas in Manitoba were designated industry which might have been attracted to our area flowed to Manitoba. In addition, the province of Manitoba at that time had a particularly vigorous development fund which worked against what we considered to be our interests.
The problem in one case was that the whole province of Nova Scotia was committed to a program of regional or provincial development, whereas in the case of large provinces like Ontario and Quebec large areas were ignored, sometimes because of internal problems within the provinces. When this new legislation is brought down I hope it will have sufficient flexibility to recognize these very real problems and distinctions that are found in the various parts of our country.
In returning to the legislation before us I should like to say that I am quite pleased with the powers given the minister under clauses 25 and 26. In particular, under clause 25, subclause 2, I am happy to see that the minister not only is given permission to cooperate with the provinces but also the clause provides for the participation of persons, voluntary groups, agencies and bodies within these regions. I say that because recently in the province of Ontario the government tabled a series of 13 regional development programs. One of these programs concerns the area of northwestern Ontario. It is entitled "A Five-Year Development Program For Northwestern Ontario", and was produced by the Northwestern Ontario Development Council.
Basically the primary recommendation of this study is that there be a public corporation strongly financed by the province to spearhead a massive effort to expand the region's economy and population. This corporation, modelled somewhat, I believe, along 
the lines of the Atlantic Development Board, would have the power to designate growth areas, general use areas, highways and roads and would have power to provide incentives for industrial expansion. It would promote a regional consciousness and spirit and encompass other activities related to the betterment of the northwestern part of Ontario. It was suggested that the executive or board of directors would be appointed half by northwestern Ontario municipalities and half by the provincial government, with capital provided, of course, by the provincial authority and/or, I would add, the federal authority because I believe it is quite clear the federal government will have to participate in this project if it goes ahead.
In our area we are also awaiting the report of an ARDA study which was commenced about two years ago under the federal-provincial ARDA agreement. When this project is completed, we hope some time in September, we expect we will have for northwestern Ontario a basis on which we can develop a sensible regional and economic development plan. I would be the first to admit that this will not solve all our problems. Indeed, I think there must be a considerable restructuring of local government into a regional form. There must be some power which has authority to control land use and bring about proper development patterns. Something must be done about the increasing multitude of municipalities with which we have to deal and which I think tend to weaken us economically, socially and politically.
In retracing my steps a little, Mr. Chairman, I should like to read to you the goals set up for the Northwestern Ontario Development Study:
1.	Northwestern Ontario should seek to increase its population as rapidly as possible.
2.	This population should be concentrated as nearly as is socially and economically possible, given the requirements for new economic activity, in as few urban centres as is possible.
3.	The region should achieve a level of socioeconomic excellence second to none.
I might say that these goals were not created by the consulting Arm which did the study but instead were the result of a series of teach-ins, if I might use that term, at the Quetico training centre and in the various communities which make up northwestern Ontario. I think these are goals to which all the people of northwestern Ontario subscribe.
I believe also that the concept of a public development corporation is accepted by the people of northwestern Ontario.
March 21, 1969

It is quite clear to me that the provincial and the federal governments have not enjoyed the very close co-operation one might expect in the growth of a new and developing economic structure in a region such as northwestern Ontario. In Ontario, at the present time, we have reached the point of absurdity in that we have the federal government's area development program operating under certain guidelines, but since this program was not accepted by the people of Ontario the provincial government was constrained 'to bring forward its program for equal opportunity. The result is that the provincial government and the federal government are both providing subsidies to industries locating all over Ontario with the exception, I believe, of within a 50-mile radius of metropolitan Toronto. Here we have the two governments not acting in concert but operating on a different basis with the consequence that neither program really has produced the results we had hoped for.
If the northwestern Ontario five-year development program is accepted by the province, it would seem to me that there would have to be very close co-ordination between the provincial and federal governments. I hope the minister will not take the attitude that was outlined in respect of ARDA. I believe one of the great defects of the ARDA program was that the areas which needed help were those which suffered most from depopulation or which suffered from an outflow of population. To some extent these areas lack the ability to self-start by producing the kind of pressure on governments which cannot easily be ignored. In addition, the problem is intensified by the great political divisions which exist within these regions. It is impossible for members of parliament and provincial members to properly represent all aspects of the areas simply because of the built-in conflicts in the size of the ridings.
I hope the minister will be much more aggressive than his predecessor. I hope he will seek out areas which require assistance and see that they are given assistance so that this development program may help them grow and make a contribution to the whole of Canada. Up until this time this has not been the case.
I do not like to be parochial in a debate of this kind. Nevertheless there is one other aspect of this matter which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. I feel that the hon. member for Hull will agree with me that this is a problem in his area also. I

Government Organization want to speak about the situation in Kenora-Rainy River because of its location on the periphery of Ontario. We are closer in some aspects to the province of Manitoba than we are to the province of Ontario. Our economic and social connections are with Manitoba but our political connections are with the province of Ontario. To some extent this is a condition which will not be solved easily. Nevertheless it is a real factor in respect of our existence in northwestern Ontario.

subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND FORESTRY, AND OTHER NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I welcome the opportunity to speak today and offer my comments on that portion of Bill C-173 dealing with the new Department of Regional Economic Expansion. It is not my intention to criticize the intent of the government in creating this new department. The idea is good. I have said so time and again when speaking to my constituents, but I am getting very impatient with the tardiness of the government in implementing some of the programs which they keep preaching about and the words of wisdom they expound which they say will cure the ills of regional disparity. The programs they are introducing are good. They were good programs under the Department of Forestry and Rural Development and the mere changing of the name is not suddenly, as if with a magic wand, going to accomplish the aims and objectives of these programs.
I have tried to take a serious interest in all phases of the government's policies with regard to rural development since coming to parliament because it was my sincere opinion

and belief that the incentive programs under the act were of real value to the provinces in the Atlantic region, especially to the province of Newfoundland where incentive programs to lift the economy are so critically required. In the six or seven months that I have been here I have tried to gather together as much information as possible with regard to the Department of Forestry and Rural Development to determine the application of its benefits to those areas of Canada where these programs are best suited.
In the past six months I have obtained considerable information in the form of pamphlets, booklets, studies and reports, each one of them compiled or written by the supposedly greatest brains in the country, stating how to overcome regional disparity and how to develop natural resources. Almost daily I receive notices of experts, professors' and scientists being brought in by the government to solve all of our problems. Mr. Chairman, the mandarins are coming! The government is stealing industrial experts from firms across the country to advise the government. Almost daily I receive copies of speeches made across the country by the Prime Minister, the minister of the department and also by those ministers who try to get into the act at every opportunity. If I quoted from all of them it would take me all day. I will quote from just a few recent ones. At the federal-provincial conference the Prime Minister stated:
A new constitution for Canada should start by stating objectives ... and one of them should be to promote equality of opportunity for all Canadians in whatever region they may live-
Yesterday the minister amplified that statement when he said that everyone should be able to earn a living comparable in standard from sea to sea. When speaking about this new department the Prime Minister also stated:
This will mean establishment of a department charged with the objectives of ensuring that people in all areas and regions of our country have as equal access as possible to the opportunities of Canada's economic development.
They have all the answers, Mr. Chairman. They have been preaching words of wisdom for many years. I have all the answers in my office, but they are only on paper. They are in beautifully bound pamphets which are written in the most glowing terms. I have pamphlets on regional planning for depressed areas, establishing new regional organizations, stimulants to social development in
March 21, 1969

slow growth regions, the Canada land inventory, water development, the role of education in rural development, the ARDA program in relation to recreation and tourism, views on rural development in Canada special study 1, special 2 and all the numbers, the second report on regional development and many more.
I have most of the incentive programs, such as incentives for industrial location, the Canada development agency, municipal development loan boards, the Atlantic Development Board, the Industrial Development Bank, and small business loans. They also have the answers on productivity in agriculture, farming and fishing. They are all on paper, Mr. Chairman. The government has its new programs and also M.M.R.A., P.F.R.A., ARDA, ADA and FRED. They have the whole family, Mr. Chairman, all on paper and maps.
Surely by now these programs have had their day in court. Royal commissions have finished their work, task forces have covered all the ground, and this is the time for action. But the government is again changing names, dialoguing the studying. Now there is a new word. The government is now interrogating.
Before doing anything about our own regions the government has gone looking for new ones. They found one in Latin America. They have gone junketing off to look at and solve the problems of other countries, but they have not solved their own. They are going to attempt to solve the problems of Venezuela, Peru, Colombia, Chile, Argentina and Brazil. But in their own backyard they are going to conduct more studies and more reviews. The government keeps insisting there is no money available to develop the poor provinces, but they have the money for foreign countries. They have money for the needs of Latin America for telecommunications, airport construction, mining, forestry and fishing equipment, hydroelectric equipment, grain storage facilities, pulp machinery, specialized aircraft, nuclear reactors, road and railway equipment and educational equipment. The government has found $75 million for a subway in Caracas, Venezuela, but they cannot afford a causeway for Prince Edward Island. They can find money for telecommunications in Latin America when communities in Newfoundland do not even have a telephone in this day and age of satellites. They keep closing down post offices in isolated communities even through they are the only source of communication. This is done to save money.
Government Organization
They can find money for the government of Paraguay to finance highway feasibility studies, to lend to the government of El Salvador for the construction of major ports. They can even find money to lend to the Central American Bank for Economic Integration to finance projects in Central America for highways, industrial parks and other things.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
Two hundred and eight and a half million dollars have gone to countries in foreign aid. It is referred to as the flow of financial resources to less developed countries. I wish I could find the river they are talking about so I could change the current.
I like the terms the government of the day use when they speak of involvement. I refer again to the Prime Minister's speech. He said that any plan will not work without the close involvement of the people on the spot-the minister called it participation of local areas-and that the department in Ottawa needs the full involvement of local people just as much as they need the federal government's help. These are empty words.
Where is the $305 million FRED program promised for western Newfoundland? It was supposed to start last fall, according to the premier of that province. Then it was supposed to start this spring, and then it was to be delayed because of the pending change of the name of the department. Now I find that the new department will have to look at a new plan for Newfoundland. But where is the report that was presented by the province of Newfoundland to the federal government? How can the people get involved when they do not know the first thing about the projects that are contemplated? How can they participate when no one has asked them to do so? Why the secrecy in respect of the report? Let the people know so they can become involved, if that is the advice of the minister.
So far as Newfoundland is concerned, FRED is dead. The people of Newfoundland have suffered another disappointment. I understand that the Prime Minister will be in the province in the near future. I hope he will give them the reasons for cancelling the FRED program. I am sure that he will tell them about their human rights, that they should have the same opportunities as everyone from sea to sea. He will dialogue, he will tell them to get involved, he will probe and he will interrogate. I hope they listen, because they are just a little fed up with promises.
March 21, 1969

Government Organization
It is not my inclination to be so critical, but the people of Newfoundland are becoming impatient. I apologize for being parochial but I just have to be. I accept the principles of this new department and suggest to the minister that in the riding of Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe there is a development potential which is tailor-made for his programs. I wish to emphasize that it has resources that will not mean handing out dollars with no return. I ask the minister to take a good, hard look at the natural resources of the province and make an investment which will return a hundredfold.
The west coast of the province of Newfoundland has resources which are not realized. It has a potential that, if exploited sensibly, could revitalize the economy of that province in all phases of development. But I hope the studies have all been done; I hope all the research is completed. We have had enough procrastination. What we need now in implementing regional economic expansion is action.

subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND FORESTRY, AND OTHER NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to say at the outset that many members on this side of the house have immense respect for the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. I am certainly one of those. Even that great character analyst, Judy LaMarsh, has had favourable words to say about the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development, the new Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, and if she had something favourable to say about him I suppose that in itself is an indication of something important. However, the fact that I have admiration, and respect for and confidence in the minister does not mean that I do not have some rather harsh and critical things to say to him.
In the first place, I take exception to the statement the minister made yesterday during the introduction of this part of the bill. The minister said that the introduction of this legislation to form the new department was a very important occasion for Canadians. I think the bill in itself means absolutely nothing. What will become important are the policies and actual work carried out by the government in the course of the next few years with respect to the problem of regional disparities, particularly in income.
There is no point in saying that the organization of the new department is important when we know full well, as the previous speaker has just said, that in the past few years we have had rather impressive-looking legislation on the books which has not been

translated into anything particularly effective. This has happened since 1964 or 1965. We know too, that the minister's predecessor in office, Maurice Sauve, seemed to show a great amount of enthusiasm and idealism for the task he had of implementing the provisions of ARDA and FRED in order to halt the decline and stagnation of many rural areas of the country. But nothing substantial ever occurred; there can be no mistake about that.
The minister is as determined as his predecessor to deal with the problem of regional disparities, and I hope he is prepared to take a new approach. It seems to me that the new approach should include the following. First of all, when speaking to the legislation the minister said that the concept of the new department is one of global planning. In so far as rural areas are concerned, one assumes and hopes this will1 include the problem of agricultural policy in Canada.
I have said on previous occasions, and I say again with all the emphasis I can muster, that nothing effective will be done in the realm of rural development and the elimination of regional disparities until the government is prepared to come forward with a meaningful agricultural income policy. Such a policy is almost completely lacking. It is true that with regard to the dairy industry there is an income policy of sorts, but with respect to western grain production there is no income stabilization policy worthy of the name. Therefore there are in western Canada many areas, districts and even regions which are suffering from low incomes. This situation has resulted from the fact that there is no agricultural income policy in Canada.
For the entire post-war period there has been one extreme in the United States, that of agricultural commodities price support without limit. In Canada there has been another extreme, that of no agricultural commodities price support. Surely between the two extremes there is a median that an enlightened government would want to endorse and implement. No matter how many programs the government implements, no matter how often it changes the name of a department or how many civil servants it hires, nothing meaningful will be done by the government to cope with rural poverty as long as farm income remains a problem. Only when the problem of low farm income is dealt with can the residue of the problem be dealt with through FRED or ARDA. Let there be no mistake about that.
March 21, 1969

I sometimes have the sinking feeling that the government-I am sure this will not be true of the minister-over the past few years has, in the introduction of new legislation setting up a department, fund or agency under a new name, sought to buy time. Civil servants are dispatched to different parts of the country to conduct surveys and studies, and when that is not enough outside consultants are hired for the same purpose. Months and years go by, and when there is no hope of any continued stalling, lo and behold a new bill appears under a new name and they start off tabula rasa. In the meantime, the people living in these areas continue to live in the same economic circumstance from which we had hoped to elevate them eight years ago.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
I hope the minister will see fit to make a concerted effort to allow less money to be diverted into studies, many of which have been meaningless in every respect, and to use the money saved from these studies for projects and programs that seek tangible and concrete improvements in local districts in these special designated areas. I tried to bring to the attention of the minister's predecessor the fact that under the ARDA and FRED programs as they operate in the Interlake district of Manitoba, part of which I represent, there had been a plethora of studies. I recall one study in particular on the fertility rates among different cohorts of mothers. This study cost a few thousand dollars and resulted in the finding that the fertility ratio among mothers in the Interlake district happened to be .3 of 1 per cent higher than in the rest of the province. A big deal that was! The $6,000 or $7,000 spent on that kind of study plus equal amounts of money spent on equally useless studies could have been saved and put to use in drainage improvements and road improvements, or added to the amount of money available for technical school construction or for manpower training in rural areas. This money could have been of immediate and direct benefit to the people in the area.
There is another point which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. I find there is something inherently contradictory in the efforts of the government to deal with the problem of rural poverty and regional disparities. I refer to their attitude to the role that can be played by existing Crown corporations and government agencies. Until now the pattern followed by the government has been to do something in the less advantaged

Government Organization regions where it is hoped that the attraction of industry would have beneficial effects. The government, through its old ADA program as well as through ARDA and FRED, has made capital grants available to any private entrepreneur and to any industry wanting to locate in a given region or district. I suppose that in many cases this has had limited success. But we do know that there are also Crown corporations in this country that, as a matter of internal management decision, have decided to pull out of a given region. Often this has had dire consequences for that region.
The prospect which faces the government, and in particular the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, when a Crown corporation leaves a region is the provision of massive amounts of capital by way of grants to attract new industry. In either case the cost to the Canadian taxpayer is not substantially different. In fact, it can be argued that a saving might result to the taxpayer if the existing operation were maintained, even if it required a subsidy.
Let us consider two specific instances, one being Air Canada's operation in Winnipeg and the other the Canadian Forces base at Rivers, Manitoba. Neither of these two places are in my constituency so I am not speaking from a local or parochial point of view. The fact remains that if it is the intention of the Department of National Defence, as was announced, to discontinue the Canadian Forces base operations at Rivers, it will mean the wiping out of 1,100 jobs for the people of that essentially rural area of Manitoba. The prospect of losing 1,100 jobs will mean, if not death, at least a high degree of economic stagnation for that part of the country. In turn, it will mean that if the new department is to live up to its name it will have to inject massive amounts of capital by way of grants to try to attract alternative industry.
I should like to ask the minister whether the thinking of the government is sufficiently crystallized to enable him to say whether, in the case where a government department or Crown agency or corporation decides to take a step which will have an immediate and direct bearing on the economic life of a region, it is envisaged that his department will have a considerable say on whether or not the other department or agency will be allowed to take such a step. I think this is a crucial factor and an important question on which the minister should try to elaborate at the first opportunity.
March 21, 1969

Government Organization [DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
There is another criticism which I should like to direct to the minister's attention. When the local representatives on the board of directors of a local co-operative, which is usually a small local industrial undertaking such as a creamery or cheese plant, decide that a particular kind of industry can operate successfully in that district-here I am speaking of areas which have been acknowledged as having less economic opportunity than designated areas in the rest of the country-I hope there will be a greater sense of urgency on the part of the officials of the new department and of the minister than was the case under the ADA program, for example. I speak from direct experience in this regard. In my area a local co-operative creamery decided that because of the changing nature of the dairy industry in Canada and in the west it would be desirable to supplement the local creamery operation with a cheese plant. After a number of local meetings in which many of the local residents involved themselves-and this type of involvement is supposed to be the essence of the whole approach-a decision was reached to go ahead with the construction of a cheese plant. It was found possible to raise between $30,000 and $40,000 locally, but a matching grant from the Department of Industry under the area incentives legislation was needed. After two years these people are still waiting for financial assistance.
I wish to emphasize that in many rural districts which are impoverished and face prospects of further decline, it takes hard thinking to come up with proposals for concrete action. It is not easy to decide what kind of industrial possibility will be feasible. But here we see an instance of local people led by their local co-operative board of directors, many of whom have a good deal of experience in business affairs. They agree on a concrete proposal involving the raising of between $30,000 and $40,000 locally and they make arrangements to provide this sum. But, when they ask the department to make use of its much publicized area incentive legislation to the extent of making a grant of a similar amount, the department refuses. One can only come away, in such a situation, with a pretty sour impression of the way in which the department handles these matters.
Only a few miles away from this community one of the largest corporations in the country has built a distillery costing about $10 million. The corporation is not impoverished,
[Mr. Schreyer.J
but in order to attract it to locate in this designated area capital grants of the order of 30 per cent of construction costs were made to it. The distillery gives work to upward of 100 people in the community, and that is fine. But in addition to outright capital grants provision is made for an accelerated capital cost allowance. Altogether, the amount of transfer capital from the taxpayers of Canada to this corporation comes to several million dollars. Yet when a band of local dairy producers wants to get $40,000 out of the government they meet with two years of stalling.
It cannot be said that the project was not feasible, that it was rash. I defy anyone to show me a group of people more cautious and prudent than local businessmen or directors of local -co-operative boards. The department has made a gracious offer. It has said that in a year or 18 months it will reconsider the application and maybe grant moneys retroactively. Bearing in mind the kind of harvest in western Canada last year, bearing in mind the decline in farming in 1968, I believe the time for action is now, not next year after what one hopes will be a fruitful harvest.
There -are many instances which one could cite without being unfair in the slightest way to show that there is something incredible about the operations of the various agencies which have been established to deal with the problem of inter-regional disparities, low rural income, and so on. When the department is presented with opportunities of concrete action in respect of concrete projects it responds by procrastination and delay.
In conclusion, I should like to say the time has come to speak with more candour than in -the past about the problem of rich and poor regions. I feel that unless the government is prepared to make greater use of existing and new Crown corporations nothing substantial will be done. There are certain approaches open to it. There is something illogical -about a situation where at a time of slow growth and high unemployment in certain regions the central government is pursuing a blanket policy of tight money and high interest rates. In some -areas this might be logical but in others it is the height of folly. I conclude by saying -there is ample opportunity for effective action by the government. I wanted to make a point about the role of fiscal and-monetary policy. It would not take too long.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am convinced that when the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development (Mr. Marchand) makes that statement, he will get the approval of every honest cabinet minister. I also hope that to ensure the success of those projects the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development will demand the co-operation of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), since only he can evaluate at this time the damage caused to Canadian businesses by excessive imports. It is useless to think of establishing or expanding plants to produce goods to fill the needs of the Canadian family if the government does not reduce those imports. Already, the electrical appliances, clothing, and shoe industries of Canada have
March 21, 1969

Government Organization been greatly affected, in Ontario and particularly in Quebec, where plants established for 50 to 75 years have recently disappeared as a result of increased imports. That means we cannot think of creating employment without taking the consumers into consideration.
It must not be forgotten that Canadian consumers will purchase only in case of need, and if they have the necessary purchasing power. Now, many unemployed who have been retrained are coming on the labour market to offer their services, and thousands of youngsters are also hoping to get jobs.
In the Ottawa area alone, 50,000 students are seeking summer jobs and according to the Manpower Centre, only 3,000 to 5,000 jobs are available, which means that 40,000 students will be unemployed during the summer.
That proves, Mr. Chairman, that skilled manpower is numerous enough in the country now to meet the demand of manufacturers.
Let us be careful not to import indiscriminately. We should not forget that no country buys from Canada to do us a favour or out of gratefulness. Events of the past are a proof of it and it is quite normal that a country buys what it needs at home and only calls upon foreign countries when it lacks some product.
Mr. Chairman, another aspect of the vocational training policy should be, in my opinion, to help farmers. Indeed, one of the main tasks of government as far as designated areas are concerned is to allow access to vocational training to farmers whether or not they are fated to remain on the farm.
If a farmer must stay on the farm, he must have the technical knowledge necessary to face the problems of managing a modem farm. On the other hand, if he must leave the farm, he should not go to the city as a castaway but he should have the necessary knowledge to practice a trade.
I trust that the rules enacted under this bill will enable the greatest number of farmers to attend the schools during the coming months.
As far as the riding of Portneuf is concerned, only 40 p. 100 of the farmers interested in further training have been allowed in recent years to attend classes that are now offered to them.
In order to control the market for their products, the farmers, through proper organizations, have tried to follow up as far as they could the movement of their products. They have also tried to organize for their benefit the sale of their products, natural or processed.

We have seen well organized co-operatives with a good system for the production, the preserving and the sale of fruits and vegetables. I have in mind particularly several areas of the province of Quebec, such as Riviere-du-Loup, Orleans Island, Quebec-Montmoren-cy, Portneuf and Saint-Jerome.
We also have cold storage facilities that were built thanks to grants from the provincial and federal governments.
