But whatever the projects under study, capital is needed to carry them out. We must not think, however, that this bill will regard all problems as pertaining to the so-called special areas.
Let us remember for example, the investments of some $15 million in Arvida, by the Aluminium Company. That company invested $15 million, the federal grant was $5 million, which makes a total investment of $20 millions and the creation of 100 jobs. Therefore, it is an investment of $200,000 per job.

Those huges investments create very few jobs, but large profits and as automation gains ground,

would promote the growth of present business concerns and the creation of new ones.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in speaking on this government reorganization bill I shall be concerned with one area only, and that is P.F.R.A. I support the general tone of the bill and its endeavour to foster better economic growth as well as to correct regional disparities. I caution, however, that although it may be easy to set up the new department, it will not be easy for this department to deal with regional disparities. After all, regional disparities exist in any economy, be it socialist, a so called free economy or a regimented economy as they have in Russia.
It has become difficult in many highly developed countries to take care of that segment of the population that has not found security within the economy of the nation. In this country, with our huge underdeveloped natural resources, we ought to be much more successful in tackling this problem and in reaching an original solution.
Government Organization
May I now speak of the matter of P.F.R.A. I believe this has been one of the more rewarding government ventures and has made possible constructive developments in the rural economy of Canada. As Canadians, we owe a debt to this vehicle which has been so useful. I am sure it has contributed much to the productive capacity of our farming community. The pattern this venture has laid down ought to be followed and built on. It has created large cadres of skilled engineers and others who are able to pass judgment, based on their experience and know-how, on programs that have been undertaken. The most visible evidence of P.F.R.A. in western Canada is the larger dams that have been constructed such as the Shellmouth Dam on the Assiniboine River in my constituency. This dam is now nearing completion and will be very useful. In addition, P.F.R.A. has been involved in many similar projects to do with water; I refer to projects such as dugouts, small run-off dams and other programs that have increased the livestock carrying possibilities of our economy.
Although most of the larger P.F.R.A. projects in western Canada have been completed, many projects in other parts of Canada remain to be undertaken. I am concerned about the fact that responsibility for implementing programs under this legislation is to be transferred to the new Department of Regional Economic Expansion. I believe that much of the effort of the new department will be expended east of Montreal and in the Maritime provinces. I approve of that, since in those areas we seem to find the greatest economic disparities.
I now wish to add a word of warning about the relation of agriculture to P.F.R.A. The government has sent out numerous task forces that are involving themselves in various programs in this country. The task force on agriculture suggested that wheat acreage should be cut by 10 million bushels and that no dairy herd of less than 30 cows should be allowed to be operated. I do not quite agree with wholesale changes such as these that the task force recommends. I wonder if many of the premises on which these surveys were conducted were not, to some extent, falacious.
It seems to me that many rural people eventually will have to leave their farms and seek their livelihood in cities. This factor, I presume, is behind the idea of establishing central areas of regional economic focus where industries could be assembled to provide jobs for displaced people. Yet much
March 21, 1969

Government Organization remains to be done for those who remain on the farms. Perhaps many will not have to leave the area in which they are living; many may change their occupation from one involving farming to one involving employment in some service industry and so continue living in rural or semi-rural surroundings. By this I mean that these people could easily involve themselves in recreational industries and other services that inhabitants of larger centres would use. There is great potential for establishing recreational industries or services in rural areas, in addition to secondary industries.
I believe that P.F.R.A. has a much greater role to play now than it ever had before; in future, it will enter more fully into the economic life of our community than it has in the past. It will work more closely with provincial governments; throughout all Western Canada and other areas of Canada, therefore, a survey into the condition of land and land use should be carried out. Although much has been done, much more remains to be done. We have been profligate with natural resources such as water, land and forest. Erosion has hurt our country considerably and will hurt it more in the future unless steps are taken to correct erosion. The work of preserving our natural topography has only just begun and we ought to press forward with this work with all reasonable speed. The preservation of wet lands has become a problem in North America and a particular problem on the prairies. Preserving this land will help us to preserve a better balance of nature. If man is to remain on this continent with any degree of success, he will have to be more careful about preserving his natural surroundings.
There is a great future for P.F.R.A. in this field, Mr. Chairman. Although the new minister will be engrossed in problems of regional economic expansion, I hope he will not lose sight of the productive potential of P.F.R.A. I should like to see the aims of this legislation increased. Although it does not deal directly with the welfare of the people, in the long run it is a very productive tool of government and will contribute much to the agricultural community. With these few remarks, Mr. Chairman, I conclude.

Mr. Chairman', there seems to be a general idea that Ontario is a prosperous province and needs no help from area development programs. In a general sense, Ontario is a prosperous province. A large proportion of the national income derives from the province of Ontario and much of

our industry is established in Ontario. In that general sense, Ontario is prosperous. Nevertheless, there are underdeveloped areas of the province which do not share in the total provincial prosperity. I want to point out that fact this afternoon.
I represent an area in the Georgian Bay region of Ontario in which, as a general rule, the inhabitants* have a reasonable standard of living. The people there are reasonably happy. All the same, there are several important areas with underdeveloped economies that I do not wish to be overlooked. It should not be thought that Ontario does not suffer from any problems connected with underdeveloped regions and that there are no provincial areas needing help.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
In that connection, a report was prepared recently by the Georgian Bay Regional Development Council, and I would like to read part of that report as it appears in the Globe and Mail of Friday, March 7 under the headline, "Prosperity Gap Greatest in Georgian Bay region". It reads:
The Georgian Bay area is in trouble, faced with a prosperity gap greater than any of the nine other provincial regions.
Over-government, collapsing industries and disappearing communities in some areas, outmoded highways and irrational development policies are its major problems, according to the report of the Georgian Bay Regional Development Council.
To remove and stabilize the 11,500 square mile area the report recommends an integrated federal-provincial development plan, a drastic reduction in the number of municipalities, a new highway development plan and the designation of urban areas as growth points

To support the claim, it publishes statistics showing that Georgian Bay is at, or next to, the bottom in comparisons of income, market ratings, industry ratings, retail sales, ten year growth rates and population growth.
Collingwood and Parry Sound are in Slow decline-
Further, on its states:
The region is perhaps a more difficult challenge than any of the problem areas of Ontario for it is not poor enough to be called an economic disaster area and, unfortunately, it is not yet in a stage of sustained, self-generating growth.
I think that fairly describes the area that I represent. It is not in any sense of the word a disaster area. In general, it has a good tourist industry. There are a number of other industries established there, yet on the west side of the district of Parry Sound, in the Georgian Bay area, there has been no benefit from the incentives that have been offered by the government in past years.
March 21, 1969

We are a designated area and the incentives that have been granted under the Area Development Agency have been used for several industries. We have been very fortunate, at least on the east side of Parry Sound and Muskoka, in establishing better economic development. However, on the west side, on the coast of the Georgian Bay, in the parts around the town of Parry Sound and north from there some 80 to 100 miles, development has fallen far behind what it ought to be.
Highly improved educational facilities and a good vocational school have been constructed in Parry Sound. In the village of Britt, which is just north of there, an excellent public school has been constructed. There has been an upgrading of the attempt to get some further economic value from the communities, but there is as yet nothing on which the young people can use their improved knowledge and special skills. The result is that those who stay there are very little better off than were their parents or grandparents. Those who leave merely increase the problems of the urban areas in housing, employment and transportation.
In most cases the offering of incentives is not sufficient in itself. There has to be an over-all joint program to meet the needs of an area. For example, several industries have given serious consideration to establishing plants in the West Parry Sound area. I would like to tell the minister, who has just come into the chamber, that I am speaking of the Georgian Bay area of Ontario.
But there are other problems which must be solved at the same time in order to bring in two or three of these industries. Natural gas is a first requirement for some industries, yet the natural gas lines were built some 40 miles further east. There is no use building the plants until the gas supply problem is met, and there is no use putting in the gas until the industries are there. This is the type of situation where a combined federal-provincial program is necessary, and I am trying to impress upon the minister that this should be a special area under the new procedures that he is going to use.
I think that the province of Ontario, which recognizes the difficulties, will be most happy to co-operate in setting up a special area in this Georgian Bay region. An expression of interest in a region by the government is a tremendous force for the better. Industry

Government Organization which has knowledge of sympathetic government support is usually willing to take a reasonable chance. Certainly designation as a special area of development would help.
I am glad that the minister is in the chamber so that once again I can tell him that the great need is to get started in this area, to get one major industry in there, and then the rest will come. Once we have got that incentive into the west Parry Sound area, I am sure that area will develop because it has a tremendous advantage in harbours. It is on the St. Lawrence-Great Lakes seaway. I pointed out it was my opinion that as the minister responsible for manpower he had adopted a very provincialistic attitude by placing manpower retraining in the provincial field again when it had been in the federal field. Since that discussion, I have had an opportunity to look at several speeches made by the minister. I should like to mention some of the programs we have had. I know they have been gone into in detail. However, in most cases in respect of ARDA and the area development agency, we have had very competent people in those departments. Considerable leadership has been provided both in the agricultural and industrial field. Yet, there has been a very small degree of success. It is true that in some areas there has been more development than in others. The situation in Brantford is a good example. This area asked to be undesignated because there were too many industries. In respect of one program with which I have been concerned, I phoned the official directly in charge who advised me that they had not been able to get the project through the counterpart provincial agency. After months and months, when the people who had been interested in the project were no longer interested in it, finally agreement was reached. It is my opinion that the development areas of Canada will be broken down into three particular regions. One region will be the area north of the St. Lawrence region. It is the area we call the Golden Horseshoe and stretches from Quebec and Montreal through to Windsor. This area is not likely to need a great deal of assistance in developing industry. This is an area where, in my opinion, more difficulty will be experienced because of industry than because of the lack of industry.
There is another area, which I believe is the one we are considering, which stretches from the Atlantic provinces through to the west coast. It might be called a mid-Canada area. In my part of the country, it is the area beginning about 50 miles north of Toronto and stretching to the tree line. If the information I have from other countries is correct, for a considerable period of time the tree line probably will mark the end of the area in which there can be secondary industrial development. There will, of course, be primary development beyond that. I think the area we are talking about is what one might call a

resource base area rather than an industrial area. This is an area which to some extent is industrialized now because of the various natural resources in the area. This is true in my part of the country. It has also affected the main centres in the south part of the area. They seem to be in a fairly viable position. In fact, the two major centres of Sault Ste. Marie and Sudbury have the highest income level in that whole area, and probably in Canada.
In these places, the secondary development has been related to the natural resources. They have been very successful in this field. Farther north, however, this has not been possible. There, there is a lack of transportation and communication facilities. The fact is that my area is 400 miles north of Toronto and it takes five days for a letter to get to Toronto. This can be very disturbing to a businessman. A doctor told me that out of 20 or 25 samples he sent to a laboratory in Toronto in his professional capacity, 15 samples were frozen and returned as unacceptable for laboratory work. This is an indication of how poor communications are.
If this reorganization is to be successful, it will be successful because the minister believes in the program. If the minister does not really believe he, as a federal member of parliament and as a federal cabinet minister, is responsible for the regional development of all Canada, then this program will not work. The program did not work in respect of ARDA, FRED and AIDA. The main reason it has not worked is that there has been a patronage arrangement either by the federal government or the provincial government. Personally, I would like to see one of the two get out of some of these fields.
The previous speaker, the hon. member who comes from Parry Sound-I doubt whether that is in northern Ontario but it is close by-made representations in respect of the tourist industry. In my area, the tourist industry has been assisted by the federal government through the area development incentive program. However, the tourist industry would seem to be much more in the provincial field since parks, reforestation, and the maintenance of stocks of fish and game are under provincial jurisdiction. Licensing also falls within the jurisdiction of the province.
I should like to see the provincial government take over the development of the tourist industry. I have no objection to the federal government providing some money in this regard, but I believe it is rather ludicrous for

both governments to be vying for the opportunity to help in this regard.
One concept of ARDA was that little groups would get together and choose a community they would help. This might take the form of the reclamation of marshland, the draining of a swamp area or the conversion of a farming area from one kind of produce to another by the building of a facility to handle the new type of produce. This concept automatically brought to the minds of both the provincial and federal politicians that the program was within their jurisdiction. Except in respect of the two major programs we have, the provincial people and the federal people did not work in conjunction with each other. Therefore, the projects were superimposed on the communities. The communities had very little co-operation from the provincial people and none from the federal people because the negotiations and arrangements were not made at the community level. The arrangements were between governments rather than individuals.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Yesterday, the hon. member for Winnipeg North pointed out the change in attitude apparent in a number of publications and statements made by the government in recent months. The same situation is developing between Manitoba and northwestern Ontario, the area represented by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall try to be brief in order to give the house the opportunity to end the debate without undue delay.
That new department has raised many hopes. As a proof, I would like to quote a journalist Mr. Roger Champoux, who wrote an article in La Presse on February 19, 1969.

The project is tremendous and the instrument to implement it has just been dratted. The federal government has thus taken on a tremendous task in establishing a super-department responsible for levelling the economic disparities of this country.
Actually, and I am saying this without any attempt at irony, the federal government is fulfilling an electoral promise, but above all, in so doing, it justifies at long last those reasonable people who have been calling for strong action and ingenious ventures to raise a number of Canadian areas out of their stagnation. This is an emergency and it has all the makings of a drama.
At this stage, Mr. Chairman', I would like to point out that the Creditistes are among the reasonable people the journalists are speaking of. We Creditistes, feel that the editorial writer, even if he did not intend to do so, was referring to us, for ever since the beginning of our campaign to get the government to deal with the economic depression, we have been laughed at and people have been saying: it is demagogy. The country is prosperous, all is well and therefore the Creditistes were demagogues. Today, in the very paper which was abusing us, one may read that reasonable people are those who have long been raising the alarm and pointing out, because it became more and more obvious, that there was an economic depression.
We are very happy about this government initiative and we hope that even if this the real solution, is not found even if once more we do not reach to the real causes, as the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Latulippe) pointed out yesterday, even if this is not the magic key to many of our problems, we will nevertheless not object to some improvement of the present system, which we reject.

And the editorial writer goes on to say:
We have lived for a long time with the illusion that the country was so rich that its normal growth would continue without major problems. But lo! Delegation to Quebec City

yards in the Quebec region, about which questions obviously come to mind.

That people who authorize degradation of our rights, Libres Entreprises, be deprived of office and replaced by others who can guarantee impartiality.

Mr. Chairman, I can assure the minister I will be very brief but I would like to add a word or two to what has been said with regard to this bill. May I remind him of a statement which he made on March 20, as recorded at page 6895 of Hansard and which reads as follows:
The first thing we have to do is establish the department before we indicate to the house exactly what we intend to do.
I admit I do not understand the minister's words. It has always been my impression that before we can ask the people of this country to expend money in establishing a department of the government, members of the house should really know what the terms of reference and intentions of that particular department are. I, therefore, ask the minister, when he rises, to answer the questions that have been asked of him and to indicate to the house exactly what his department intends to 4o in the immediate future. I realize the
IMr. Matte.]
department must be established before he can possibly speak with authority. Nevertheless, I believe members of this house are entitled to have an understanding of exactly what the department intends to do. At the same time, I believe his department faces the greatest challenge of any department that is being established under this bill. I know the minister in charge of housing has suggested that everyone in this country should have an opportunity to choose the type of home in which he would like to live. However, before this can possibly happen, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion must improve the economy of this country and make it possible for everyone to have that choice. I believe that this free choice is a great myth until disparities in different parts of Canada are corrected. We know that there is a disparity in wages throughout Canada, and this again will have to be tackled by a department of the government.
I should like to quote another portion of the minister's opening address at page 6894 of Hansard. It reads as follows:
-the department's goal will be to ensure that economic growth is dispersed widely enough across Canada to bring employment and earnings opportunities in the hitherto slow growth regions as close as possible to those in the rest of the country.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I suggest to the minister that in his attempt to bring this about he should not forget to consider the situation of areas which are steadily going down, areas which have dry rot at their roots. There are many such communities throughout Canada, and perhaps I can use Moose Jaw as an example. This is a city which has suffered severe hardship through the loss of many industries; we are close to the capital city. Even though outward appearances might indicate a prosperous community, there is a rot developing at the very core and if it is not attended to under the terms of the new legislation I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that conditions in the area will not be pleasant in* the future. I ask the minister to pay attention not only to areas which are suffering today, but to the situation in areas which will suffer, and suffer deeply, if no consideration is given to their needs.
I notice the minister also says:
This bill provides for the establishment of special areas when employment opportunities are very limited in the region itself or in the territory of which that region is a part.
I should welcome an explanation of some of these terms, specifically a definition of "territory". Perhaps we could be given a definition
March 21, 1969	COMMONS
of what will constitute growth areas or special areas, and told how this is likely to be interpreted in the regulations. We would then be able to establish whether there is any meat in the bill, because it is these regulations which will determine whether the necessary action can be taken.
I agree with my hon. friend who spoke earlier that this should be a federal matter. If this bill is to mean anything to the Canadian people as a whole, too much reliance should not be placed on the idea of co-operation between governments at federal and provincial levels. It scarcely seems likely that the two levels of government can move quickly enough to remedy the situation which this country faces.
I ask the minister not to be too much taken up with this idea of really close co-operation in carrying out this work. Everyone agrees there must be co-operation. But if we wait for co-operation before taking any action, well laid plans can go astray, for political or other reasons. I believe the hon. member for Timis-kaming was correct when he said the federal government must itself accept responsibility for putting the provisions of this bill into effect.
I respectfully urge the minister to see that regulations are drawn up which will make this bill a meaningful part of our institutions. Everywhere in Canada people are looking to this new department trusting it will do something for their areas. I can appreciate the situation in which the minister finds himself, but if he works diligently to ensure that every part of our nation is taken into consideration, I am sure he will earn our congratulations. The special areas will, of course, have to be given special treatment. I wish the minister success in his new department and again suggest he urge his colleagues and every member of his staff to take the entire nation into consideration when laying plans and drawing up the regulations to make this legislation effective.

speechtext:
My first words will be words of thanks to the members of the committee for their contribution to the debate. Most of the speeches were instructive. Everyone appeared conscious that this is a serious question, one with which we have had to deal as Canadians ever since confederation, and probably before.
Up to now, nobody has succeeded in solving this problem. Those who tell me that I am not likely to succeed are, of course, on safe ground. They are conservative, and I do not say they will be proved wrong, since history tells us that all those who have tried to deal with it have failed. Will it be different this time? I do not know. The only thing I can say today is that given the instruments provided by this legislation I shall try as hard as I can. After that, the house can judge whether or not I have been successful.
I thank the committee for its co-operation. As so many hon. members emphasized, this is a difficult task and it will not be accomplished overnight. I do not want those who live in underdeveloped regions to think I shall be able to perform miracles once this law is passed and that overnight they will become prosperous. I know that is not true. Many governments have been in power in Ottawa since confederation and none of them has been successful in this field. Provincially, it has been the same story. Some premiers and provincial governments have tried hard, and they have been successful to a certain extent in dealing with this problem, but it is still with us today. I know exactly what I am trying to tackle. I have no illusions, and I know the house has no illusions. But I believe that if we receive co-operation from every part of the country we can increase the pace of progress in this field and do better than in the past. If we are successful in achieving this, I shall be satisfied and could probably retire at the age of 90 or 95.
The hon. member for Egmont said he would like to know, at least in a general way, what the department intends to do. I thought this over, and found it a reasonable enough request. I shall try not to go into details of
March 21, 1969

Government Organization the program we are presently studying, because the cabinet is still at work on the first bill we intend to bring forward in connection with incentives to industries. However, I think I can say in broad terms in what direction we are moving.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Hon. members have emphasized the importance of consultation with the provinces. Certainly, we will have to consult. I respect the importance of consultation. Equally, I respect the authority of parliament. Until parliament has given me the powers requested in this bill, I do not think it would be right for me to enter into consultation with the provinces on detailed plans. On the one hand, I am asked to consult with the provinces; on the other hand, I am asked, before any consultation has taken place, to give the details of what we are going to do. Until I have consulted the provinces I am not going to talk publicly about particular plans; this would make a mockery of consultation.
However, I am happy to take this opportunity to describe to hon. members, and to the public, the broad outlines of the programs I propose to pursue. The first program is to improve opportunities for industrial employment. For that purpose, I will be introducing to the house in May, I hope, legislation on industrial incentives to replace the existing ADA legislation. The new program will be considerably different from the present one, and I believe will be much more effective in creating new, permanent and viable employment. This program will be especially important for Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and eastern Quebec, though it will be of considerable importance to slow growth areas in all provinces.
At this point, I should like to inform hon. members that in all of the programs we are studying we do not intend to deprive any region of Canada of the benefit of the law presently in force. In other words, we are not going to give less than we are giving now. Some hon. members expressed the fear that a new program might take out some regions which then would not be in as good a position as they are today as a result of the new legislation. This is not our intention; we are trying to improve what is in existence today, not destroy what is good.
Second, I will be seeking to work out with the provinces, plans for the development of the main centres within the regions where economic growth has hitherto been slow. We will be offering federal resources to help
[Mr. Marchand (Langelier) .1
these centres respond to growth opportunities. So far we have FRED plans for rural development, and this is important. I am proposing to extend that approach to plans for urban economic and social development.
Third, I will be proposing a series of plans to encourage and help the development of medium sized and small towns as trading centres and smaller industrial centres. That is especially important to the prairies, though of course it applies to eastern Canada too.
Fourth, I hope we can join with the provinces and local groups in formulating a series of plans for development and adjustment in rural areas of eastern Canada. We inherit the Gaspe plan, the plans for northeastern New Brunswick and for the Mactaquac area. They are not working perfectly. There are a lot of difficulties and we have to learn by experience. I will not be offering instant new plans. Quite a bit of time will be needed to perfect our programs. But we will be working as fast as it is possible to work effectively.
To those who raised this question, may I say we do not intend to set up royal commissions or task forces. We want to experiment with new programs and see how they work in each case.
Fifth, the P.E.I. plan, covering a whole province, is a special case. I shall be aiming to add another special case as soon as possible, because I think we need a distinctive plan for economic and social development to meet the particular needs of Newfoundland.
Some hon. members expressed the opinion a few minutes ago that there should be general plans throughout Canada. I do not think there should. Problems that are encountered in P.E.I. or Nova Scotia, in northern Quebec or northern Ontario, are not the same. If we want to make progress in this field we shall have to accept reality and plan specifically to meet the needs of the regions we want to help.
Sixth, there are the areas of Canada where Indian and Metis people are a large proportion of the population. They encounter particularly large obstacles to fully sharing in Canada's development. I propose to mount, again of course with provincial co-operation and local involvement, special plans to combat the problems of such areas.
Seventh, I referred a minute ago to a special plan for Newfoundland. In that plan, improved transportation must be an important element. For Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, we will need a long-range transportation plan that will include a program of
March 21. 1969	COMMONS
federal assistance for trunk highways as well as federal action for some major port developments.
I think one point that was raised many times during the debate was some hon. members were afraid that what we were spending now, partly through the Atlantic Development Board, on infrastructures would be eliminated in future. This is not true. I hope we will spend more than we have been spending for this purpose under A.D.B., because there is no doubt in my mind that it is useless to think of economic development for certain regions or cities if the infrastructures in those regions or cities are not built or rebuilt. Therefore, we require authority to do this. It is clear from the statute that public works and facilities are available to this end. As I say, we do not intend to do less than the A.D.B. used to do in the maritimes; I hope it will be more, much more.
Eighth, there are the programs of resource development on the prairies that we inherit through P.F.R.A. and, to a considerably lesser extent, ARDA. I intend in time to develop such programs, and to co-ordinate them with social programs such as we have in the FRED plan for the interlake area of Manitoba.
As hon. members know, this bill is not
going to put a term to P.F.R.A.; we are going to work with this program and I hope we can improve it. Perhaps later on we will think of something else, but let us wait and see how we progress with the present plan.
Ninth, we are also making through ARDA a contribution to rural resource development and rationalization in Ontario and British Columbia. We will be seeking to work with the provinces to make such programs more effective.
Finally, we will be working with the provinces in certain areas where tourism offers one of the main prospects for improved employment and earnings. Those are the then headings under which we will be developing our programs. A great deal of detailed planning has to be done, joint planning that takes time. A great deal of money will also have to be found.
I entirely agree with members opposite who (suggested that the department is, in effect, merely a framework. There is no doubt about that. This gives us a better chance to make our programs more effective. If the programs are good, then over the next few years 1hey will require increasing priority in terms of expenditure. However, I think

One of my problems will be, of course, to find the money required. The other main problem, as several hon. members have rightly pointed out, will be to get the co-operation of other ministers and departments. There is no doubt that this will be a difficult problem, and this was underlined many times both in the committee and here in this house. While some mistakes have been made, I think some hon. members, and also some members of the public at large, have assumed I have more power than actually granted by this bill. It is underlined throughout the bill that any important program to be carried out must be approved by the Governor in Council. The minister therefore has no personal power. I say that bearing in mind the late Hon. C. D. Howe. Unquestionably he had great power. I make these remarks, not because I do not have the greatest respect for the late C. D. Howe but because we do not have the same backgrounds. Surely, he was a man who had great power; but it was personal power and not derived from law.

Then, if I may, I will not deal with all those particular cases that I shall examine later on, and if we can do something to settle them, we will be very happy to do it.
Yet some problems were referred to, about which I would like to give some precisions. If I am allowed to, I shall start with the remarks of the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) who in fact is very conversant with the problem of regional disparities since he experienced them probably more than I did, and since he is fully aware of this critical situation. I totally agree with him upon the proposed solutions, yet though he is probably not better than I am at working miracles, I think he is good in his part and that he brings a very valuable contribution to this debate.
He raised problems that are perhaps irrelevant, say, in a technical way, when speaking of the "causeway".
Mr. Chairman, I hope the figures on which the government based its refusal to build the causeway will be at the disposal of the house or of the committee on transport and communications, so that all those directly involved in this debate, even if they interpret those figures differently, will understand why we took a decision as important as this one.

I think he knows very well that taking the total amount of each party's contribution, meaning $500 million to be provided by Prince Edward Island as against the relatively modest contribution of $225 million from the federal government, is not a very fair way to present the problem, for either one of the parties, in fact, included [Mr. Marchand (Langelier) .1
in this sum of $500 million from Prince Edward Island is a large portion of its regular budget, meaning that several things that have been included in the project are part of the normal services and activities of the province, of which we pay about 60 per cent of the budget through the tax equalization program.
And so, in any case, I do not believe it is right to consider only the two figures and to say that in a joint program with a small province, the federal government contributes only $225 million, whereas the provincial government contributes $500 million.
I think that even if the figures are correct, the facts are altogether different. I do not think that any Canadian government, even if that were his ideal, could do as much for the whole of Canada as we are doing through FRED for Prince Edward Island. In fact, our contribution is the equivalent of $2,000 per capita. If the same scale were used for the province of Qubec, can you imagine what it would give for all the other provinces?
Obviously, it may not be enough, but I believe that the program deserves to be attempted honestly. However, to present the problem as it was presented is not altogether fair, for I think that our contribution is much larger than the figures seem to indicate.
The question of co-operation with the provinces was also brought up. You will have noticed in the text of the legislation-to which an amendment will be proposed'

that we want co-operation. And in spite of the theories put forward by some hon. members of the New Democratic party, who want a united Canada, without taking into account jurisdictions, I maintain that it is impossible to do any economic planning in Canada without the co-operation of the provinces and that of the communities, through the provinces, or even without the co-operation of private enterprise and voluntary organizations.
It is being too optimistic to think that the federal government can, by itself, do economic planning when its spending power throughout Canada is now lower than that of the provinces and municipalities.
Therefore, it is obvious that if we work to develop an area, while the province works in an opposite direction, the results will cancel one another, because co-operation is imperative and should not remain a dead letter. I think that we all agree on that point.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to move an amendment to this clause. Before I do, I should like to say that the minister has supported my amendment by saying that consultation or co-operation with the provinces would be carried out. My amendment is to the effect that after the words "council may" shall be added the words "after consultation with the province or provinces". The minister has supported my argument in respect of this amendment. It is absolutely essential that the provinces be consulted so far as the Atlantic area is concerned. This may be less crucial in respect of the maritimes since the bill provides for the establishment of an Atlantic Council through which the department might carry on consultation, but in the absence of information concerning how much power this council will have I feel this amendment protects the interests of the Atlantic provinces. There are, however, other regions which are concerned such as parts of Ontario, Quebec and the western provinces. They also come under the jurisdiction of this bill.
Unless other amendments are introduced, there will be no regional councils which would be able to carry the views of these regions to Ottawa. Within these provinces there might be development plans in respect of certain areas or counties which might not be in accord with what the federal government has in mind. I suspect the provinces have priorities in respect of development. It is for this reason they must be consulted.
Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Battle River:
-that in clause 24 after the words "council may" the following words be added, "after consultation with the province or provinces".

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, here we are defining the way in which the minister is going to be able to carry out his functions in terms of the plans for economic expansion in particular. One of the problems
DEBATES	6987
Government Organization which concerns members in all parts of the house is not being sure that one of the critical areas of co-ordination in fact occurs effectively.
We know in the first instance a number of departments or parts of departments and agencies have been brought under this new department, and others with respect to regional development have been created. We also recognize this has been a weakness right through the piece of legislation. If programs and plans of other departments are not effectively tailored, the benefits achieved from the actions of this particular department will be minimal to say the least. The minister indicated that he presumably will have some form of veto power, with regard to the cancellation of certain kinds of programs, such as military installations or perhaps public works projects.
What we are talking about here is something much more important to the day by day workings of government administration and particularly the on-going design of fiscal and monetary policies. Under the old FRED set-up there was established a FRED board. I think that one provision relating to the FRED board was that ten senior officials would meet. It was a fairly structured affair that had application to the design and implementation of FRED plans. That board has been shelved, of course, because the FRED legislation as such is disappearing. I think what was being attempted under that program was the whole business of effectively co-ordinating under this minister and his department, policies of the federal government that would encourage rather than discourage regional development. That is the kind of business we are about.
I shall, therefore, move an amendment to add a new subclause (c) to this clause. The subclause would spell out specifically, but not so specifically that it would limit or prevent the minister doing the kind of things necessary to achieve that end, the kind of device which I think will be useful if this department is to achieve the purposes the minister has outlined. I, therefore, move the addition of a new subclause (c) to clause 25 as follows:
(c) preside over a co-ordinating council consisting of senior officials of departments or agencies which in the opinion of the Governor in Council have responsibility for policies or programs affecting economic expansion and social adjustment. This council shall endeavour to advise and coordinate policies and programs with a view to achieving a measure of national economic and social equality.

It would be wrong, I think, to provide in such a legislation that a minister is to chair a committee composed of officials of other departments. We would then confuse things. I am sure there will be an interdepartmental committee to study these matters; so it is a matter of internal economy. The government has the responsibility to set up committees, and this is essential, if the legislation is to be efficient. Therefore, I shall always be opposed to the introduction of such a provision.

Mr. Chairman, I can accept that the minister might have some objection to this particular suggestion, but I think the level of objection he has registered is more emotional, if I may put it that way, than anything that could be considered as being in the nature of logic.
[DOT] <5:10 p.m.)
The essence of what is being attempted in this amendment is to make known that there will be some definite machinery not just the good will of the minister or the occasional urging of some of his senior officials. We have learned in the past that this has not been terribly effective. The fact that the FRED board is being abandoned indicates, I suppose, that it also has not been terribly effective, although the minister has not said this. I think a government which only a little more than two years ago instituted such a board in the legislation could not have suddenly concluded that the basic ideas it had were all bad. I think both this chamber and the people of this country have a right to know in what ways a problem will be dealt with. This is a great problem and cannot be glossed over by saying the minister would not feel very comfortable. The argument used by the minister against the institution of some form of machinery, which will undoubtedly be needed, can hardly be said to be convincing.
I do not think anyone here should underestimate the importance of having such machinery clearly spelled out, even in a statute, if we are going to convince the many little empires that we know develop in a bureaucracy as large as the one which must deal with the peoples of this country, that it would be
.[The Deputy Chairman.]
effective in overcoming a problem that is so thoroughly entrenched in our whole economic makeup. The attitude of these Empires will not in any way be altered simply because nine bits and pieces of other departments are suddenly appearing together under one department along with new bits and pieces that are being added. I think there must be, in the context of this legislation, a cleareut statement on the machinery which will be used1 in order not only that the minister and his department but that all departments know that the government is ultimately serious about dealing with the problems of regional disparity.
I think the minister's answer to me is not a sufficient one. I am prepared to present a counter suggestion which will really carry some weight, but I think it must be included in the legislation.

I see here the President of the Treasury Board, and I am reminded very vividly of the difficulties which we had in the designation of Saint John, Halifax and Fredericton to which I referred a minute ago. Certain criteria were set up, I understand, and it was admitted on one or two occasions that many of the officials involved were in favour of including these cities under one of the clauses, which could have been done by stretching an interpretation. I said 'this in the house, and the minister knows I stood up many times and said it. I gave him credit for being straightforward about it, but I still feel that if he had not taken a rigid position against those cities there would have been time to take some action with regard to them later when it was pointed out to him and to everyone concerned that a designation was necessary.
In my opinion, this amendment will detract from the arbitrary powers of one man who, for different reasons, may become prejudiced against an area. For that reason, I think that this amendment will enable us to avoid some mistakes of this nature that were made in the past.

Reference has been made to the danger of a minister acquiring a prejudice against a person, or an institution or a community. I hasten to assure the committee that I have not acquired, nor do I have, any prejudice against St. John's or Halifax. The hon. gentleman suggested that by stretching the interpretation of the law his wishes could have been granted. He criticizes me, perhaps, as being prejudiced because I did not go along with that stretching. However, possibly this is irrelevant to the subject under discussion.
As the hon. member for Selkirk has just pointed out, the notion that a minister can preside over a department made up of officials from other government departments and reach conclusions which would govern those other departments really offends the whole idea of cabinet government and the structure in which we operate. A department must be responsible to and responsive to the minister of that department. Ministers can only operate in relation to other departments through the minister, not by way of a short circuit to officials. As hon. members are aware, the current system for securing co-ordination is through operational and functional committees of the cabinet where there is co-ordination between departments conducted at ministerial level. It would be a very curious arrangement indeed were a minister to preside over a committee of officials, senior or otherwise, from a number of other government departments with a view to co-ordinating the efforts of all departments concerned. As my colleague has pointed out, we already have an apparatus which functions satisfactorily. It is sufficient, I think, to overcome prejudices which might be supposed to exist

I spoke last evening on this bill, and if I said anything at all it was exactly this, that the minister will have to depend on the co-operation of other departments in dealing with problems. It is not a problem that the minister of regional economic expansion can solve himself; it is a problem for the cabinet, indeed for the whole government and the House of Commons.
Let me just give an example of what I mean. I have been pushing for the extension of runway facilities in Gander. The Minister of Transport has been hedging about this for weeks and months, which is what he wants. I have written letters both to him and to his parliamentary secretary but have received no co-operation. I have talked with the Minister of Public Works about the matter, but he does not seem to know what the problem of regional disparity is all about.
I should like to ask the minister a question. In the event that the minister is not totally in favour of this particular amendment that has been proposed, and which perhaps has not been given the required consideration, will the minister be willing to concede that some provision should be made to allow for the tying together of government departments in some co-ordinated manner in order to give the minister some leverage? If he is not willing to accept the amendment, will he agree to have it stand so that, if necessary, he can come back with an amendment basically along the same lines? This is the most important clause in the whole bill because the department will either succeed or fall on it, and it may well be where the government falls.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I have the honour to inform the house that a message has been received from the Senate informing this house that the Senate have passed Bill S-23, an act to amend the Canada Shipping Act, and Bill S-29, an act respecting the production and conservation of oil and gas in the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories, to which concurrence of this house is desired.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Has
the President of the Treasury Board any amendments to make on the order of business for Monday?

Mr. Speaker, on Monday I think, not having completed this bill today on its tenth day, as I understand, we will commence with the bill relating to amendments to the Superannuation Acts, Bill C-178, to be followed by item No. 62, an act respecting maritime freight rates. Following that we will take item No. 56, an act to amend the Financial Administration Act. Thereafter, the business will be as previously outlined by the President of the Privy Council for Monday. It is to be expected that Tuesday and Wednesday would be allotted days. With respect to the program for Thursday, I think the government house leader would want to consult about that again, having regard to progress made.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
